short: Eight months of night bombing that killed some 43,000 British civilians.
full:
Having failed to win air superiority over southern England, the Luftwaffe switched its effort from airfields to cities. London was bombed on 57 consecutive nights from 7 September 1940. Coventry was struck on 14 November by more than 500 aircraft navigating on radio beams, which destroyed the cathedral and much of the city centre; Clydebank, Hull, Plymouth, Liverpool and Belfast followed. Roughly a million London houses were damaged or destroyed, and around 43,000 civilians were killed across Britain.

Night defence was close to useless at first. Airborne interception radar, radar-directed anti-aircraft fire and the Beaufighter improved matters through the spring of 1941. The bombing neither broke morale nor halted war production, and the campaign ended on 11 May 1941 when the bomber units moved east for the invasion of the Soviet Union. The conclusion drawn in London — that bombing a population hardened it rather than broke it — did not prevent the far heavier campaigns later flown against Germany and Japan.
